entries.title: Eligibility and conditions for taking input tax credit
entries.summary: The gateway provision for input tax credit. It grants the entitlement in s.16(1), then fences it with cumulative conditions in s.16(2), a depreciation bar in s.16(3) and a time limit in s.16(4)–(6). 2026 settled the validity of s.16(2)(c) — the 'supplier must have paid' condition — at the Supreme Court, but the courts still disagree on how it may be applied to honest buyers.

text.t: Every registered person shall, subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in section 49, be entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business and the said amount shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger of such person.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, no registered person shall be entitled to the credit of any input tax in respect of any supply of goods or services or both to him unless,— (a) he is in possession of a tax invoice or debit note issued by a supplier registered under this Act, or such other tax paying documents as may be prescribed; (aa) the details of the invoice or debit note referred to in clause (a) has been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and such details have been communicated to the recipient of such invoice or debit note in the manner specified under section 37; (b) he has received the goods or services or both [Explanation: deemed receipt where goods are delivered, or services provided, to another person on the direction of the registered person — 'bill-to-ship-to']; (ba) the details of input tax credit in respect of the said supply communicated to such registered person under section 38 has not been restricted; (c) subject to the provisions of section 41, the tax charged in respect of such supply has been actually paid to the Government, either in cash or through utilisation of input tax credit admissible in respect of the said supply; and (d) he has furnished the return under section 39.

(i) Goods received in lots/instalments — credit on receipt of the last lot. (ii) Where the recipient fails to pay the supplier the value plus tax within 180 days from the invoice date (other than reverse-charge supplies), the ITC availed is to be paid back with interest under section 50. (iii) The recipient becomes entitled to the credit again on making the payment to the supplier.

Where the registered person has claimed depreciation on the tax component of the cost of capital goods and plant and machinery under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, the input tax credit on the said tax component shall not be allowed.

A registered person shall not be entitled to take input tax credit in respect of any invoice or debit note for supply of goods or services or both after the thirtieth day of November following the end of financial year to which such invoice or debit note pertains or furnishing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier.

Notwithstanding sub-section (4), for invoices/debit notes of FYs 2017-18, 2018-19, 2019-20 and 2020-21, ITC may be taken in any return under section 39 filed up to 30 November 2021. [Inserted by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, retrospectively from 1 July 2017]

Where registration is cancelled under section 29 and later revoked (under section 30 or by order of the Appellate Authority, Tribunal or court), and the ITC was not already time-barred under sub-section (4) on the date of cancellation, ITC may be taken in a return filed (i) up to 30 November following the FY / annual return, whichever is earlier; or (ii) for the period from the (effective) date of cancellation till the revocation order, where the return is filed within 30 days of the revocation order — whichever is later. [Inserted by Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, retrospectively from 1 July 2017]

entries.textNote: Text reproduced for study as amended to date to the best of our verification; sub-sections (5)–(6) and provisos are condensed. Always confirm against the CBIC Taxinformation portal before quoting in a reply or appeal.

interpretation.h: 1. Right or concession? The starting point
p: Section 16(1) uses the word entitled, which taxpayers rely on to argue that ITC is a vested right once the conditions are met (the CENVAT-era line from Eicher Motors v. Union of India (SC, 1999)). Revenue relies on the opposite line: in Jayam & Co. (SC, 2016, under TNVAT) and Union of India v. Bharti Airtel (SC, 2021, under GST) the Supreme Court treated ITC as a concession that is available only on the terms the statute sets.

Practical reading: once credit has been validly taken, it is protected; but whether it was validly taken depends strictly on each condition in s.16(2). Courts will not relax a statutory condition on equity alone — the arguments that win are about how the condition is applied, not whether it exists.

interpretation.h: 2. The cumulative gate in s.16(2)
p: The opening words 'Notwithstanding anything contained in this section … unless' make every clause a separate pre-condition. Failing any one is enough to deny the credit, which is why departmental notices usually list several clauses together.

(a) Document — tax invoice/debit note or prescribed document (Rule 36). (aa) Reflection — supplier has filed GSTR-1/IFF and it appears in the recipient's GSTR-2B (since 1 Jan 2022, Rule 36(4) allows no credit beyond 2B). (b) Receipt — actual or deemed (bill-to-ship-to). (ba) Not restricted — the s.38 statement does not block it (e.g., new registrants, suppliers with return defaults). (c) Tax paid by supplier. (d) Return filed by the recipient.

interpretation.h: 3. Section 16(2)(c): where the law stands on 23 November 2026
p: Validity is settled for now. The Gujarat High Court in Maruti Enterprise v. Union of India (1 May 2026) upheld s.16(2)(c), reading it together with s.41(2), s.53, s.155 and Rule 37A. The Supreme Court dismissed three SLPs against that judgment in Bhandari Scrap Traders v. Union of India (24 July 2026). Commentators note the order dealt with constitutional validity and did not lay down a rule for chain supplies.

Application is still contested. The Tripura High Court in Sahil Enterprises (6 Jan 2026) did not strike the clause down but read it down: it should not be used against a purchaser in a bona fide transaction, only where the deal is collusive or fraudulent. The Supreme Court's order in Bhandari Scrap Traders did not set that judgment aside, and an SLP against it has been reported — check its status before relying on it. The Punjab & Haryana High Court, deciding 424 petitions in Shaurya Alloys (1 Oct 2026), took a middle path: the clause is valid and is not read down, but it cannot be used as a standalone, mechanical ground, and the court issued guidelines requiring it to be applied together with ss.41, 73, 74, 75(12), 76, 79, 155 and Rules 36, 37A and 88C.

What this means in a reply to a notice: (i) do not argue unconstitutionality — that argument is closed; (ii) argue the burden — under s.155 the purchaser must prove eligibility, and State of Karnataka v. Ecom Gill Coffee Trading (SC, 2023) shows what proof looks like (invoices, e-way bills, transport, payment through bank, physical movement); (iii) argue the sequence — Suncraft Energy (Cal HC, SLP dismissed Dec 2023) and the P&H guidelines expect the department to first pursue the defaulting supplier; (iv) in the Tripura jurisdiction, plead the reading-down directly.

interpretation.h: 4. Payment to the supplier within 180 days
p: The second proviso is separate from clause (c): it is about the recipient paying the supplier. If the recipient has not paid value plus tax within 180 days of the invoice, the credit must be added to output liability with interest (Rule 37, reported in GSTR-3B), and it can be re-claimed when payment is made. Reverse-charge supplies and certain deemed supplies are excluded.

interpretation.h: 5. The time limit in s.16(4)–(6)
p: The deadline is tied to the financial year to which the invoice pertains, not the date of receipt or booking. It ends on 30 November after that FY, or on filing the annual return if earlier (substituted by Finance Act, 2022). The Patna HC (Gobinda Construction, 2023) and Andhra Pradesh HC (Thirumalakonda Plywoods, 2023) upheld s.16(4) as a valid, mandatory condition.

For reverse charge on supplies from unregistered persons, Circular 211/05/2024-GST explains that the relevant FY is that of the invoice the recipient issues under s.31(3)(f). Sections 16(5) and 16(6), inserted retrospectively by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, give relief for FYs 2017-18 to 2020-21 and for cases where registration was cancelled and later restored. Circular 237/31/2024-GST lays down how orders already passed can be rectified, but s.150 of that Finance Act bars refunds of tax already paid or credit already reversed.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction with ss.17 and 18
p: Meeting s.16 is necessary but not sufficient: s.17 restricts credit for exempt or non-business use and blocks the items in s.17(5). After Chief Commissioner v. Safari Retreats (SC, 3 Oct 2024) applied a functionality test to 'plant or machinery' in s.17(5)(d), Parliament amended the clause retrospectively from 1 July 2017 through the Finance Act, 2025 — a clear example of the law being changed to undo a judgment. Section 18 covers credit on new registration and on change of scheme (ITC-01, ITC-02, ITC-03).

interpretation.h: 7. Risk map for practitioners
p: Most s.16 demands in 2025–26 come from three data mismatches: GSTR-3B credit claimed above GSTR-2B (Rule 88D / DRC-01C intimations), suppliers' credits that were cancelled retrospectively (s.16(2)(c) and (aa)), and credit claimed after the time limit (s.16(4)). Run a monthly 2B-to-3B reconciliation, check vendors' return-filing status, keep proof that goods moved, and build GST-withholding or indemnity terms into vendor contracts.

entries.old1961: Section 3 (previous year) and section 2(9) (assessment year), Income-tax Act, 1961
entries.summary: The single biggest conceptual change in the new Act. 'Previous year' and 'assessment year' are replaced by one term: the tax year, which is the financial year from 1 April. A business or income source that starts mid-year has a shorter first tax year, running from the start date to 31 March.

text.t: For the purposes of this Act, “tax year” means the twelve months period of the financial year commencing on the 1st April.

In the case of a business or profession newly set up, or a source of income newly coming into existence in any financial year, the tax year shall be the period beginning with— (a) the date of setting up of such business or profession; or (b) the date on which such source of income newly comes into existence, and ending with the said financial year.

entries.textNote: Text as published on the Income Tax Department's site (Income-tax Act, 2025, as amended by the Finance Act, 2026).

interpretation.h: 1. One period instead of two
p: Under the 1961 Act, income was earned in a previous year and assessed in the following assessment year, so FY 2025-26 income was 'AY 2026-27'. Section 3 removes the second label: income earned from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 is simply tax year 2026-27, and it is taxed for that same tax year. Section 4 then charges tax on the total income of the tax year at the rates set by a Central Act — the Finance Act, 2026 is the first to prescribe rates under Act 30 of 2025.

The substance has not changed: since AY 1989-90, the 1961 Act already required a uniform financial-year previous year. The reform is about terminology and fewer errors (in returns, challans, notices and contracts), not about a new accounting period.

interpretation.h: 2. A shorter first year for new businesses and new income sources
p: Section 3(2) keeps the old rule: when a business or profession is set up, or a new source of income comes into existence, during a financial year, the first tax year runs from that date to 31 March. It can be one day long, and it can never be longer than twelve months — there is no option for an extended first period.

The trigger is the date of setting up, not commencement. The 1961-Act case law on this carries over because the wording is the same in substance: a business is set up when it is ready to commence (Western India Vegetable Products, Bom HC 1954); the first steps in the business, such as acquiring raw material, can mark setting up (Saurashtra Cement, Guj HC 1973); a mere decision or preparatory steps are not enough (Prem Conductors, Guj HC 1977); a service business can be set up before any revenue is earned (ESPN Software India, Del HC 2008). The date matters because expenses incurred after setting up are revenue deductions in that first tax year, while costs incurred before it generally go to capital or to the preliminary-expense provisions.

interpretation.h: 3. Transition: which Act applies?
p: Section 536 repeals the 1961 Act but saves it for earlier periods. The Department's own FAQ says the 2025 Act applies from tax year 2026-27, while the 1961 Act continues to apply to tax year 2025-26 and earlier. So a return for FY 2025-26 filed in 2026 is still filed for 'AY 2026-27' under the old Act — which is why CBDT's Circular 07/2026 extending due dates refers to section 139 of the 1961 Act.

Two practical traps: (i) proceedings for old years — assessment, reassessment, appeal and penalty — continue under the old provisions, but where a default or refund arises after 1 April 2026 the new Act's procedure may apply, so check the savings clause for each step; (ii) documents drafted before 2026 that refer to an 'assessment year' should be read against the corresponding tax year — update templates for engagement letters, loan covenants, Form 15G/H-type declarations and board resolutions.

interpretation.h: 4. Periods other than the tax year
p: Section 3 is the default, not an absolute rule. Section 4(4) allows the Act to charge tax on income of a period other than the tax year — the successors to the 1961 Act's special cases for shipping income of non-residents, persons leaving India, AOPs/BOIs formed for a particular event, persons likely to transfer property to avoid tax, and discontinued businesses. In those cases tax may be assessed before the tax year ends.

interpretation.h: 5. Checklist for the first tax year (2026-27)
p: Change your ledgers, invoices, TDS/TCS records and client communications to refer to 'tax year 2026-27'. Use the new form numbers under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 (notified 20 March 2026) for that year, and the old forms for 2025-26 compliance. For clients starting a business or a new source of income in 2026-27, record the date of setting up with evidence (for example, the date a factory became ready, an office opened, or the first lease began).

entries.title: Definitions of “goods” and “services”
entries.summary: The two definitions that decide which side of the line every supply falls on. 'Goods' is all movable property except money and securities, but expressly includes actionable claims; 'services' is the residue — anything that is not goods, money or securities. The Supreme Court's Gameskraft ruling (27 May 2026) has made the actionable-claim limb of s.2(52) the most litigated words in the definition clause.

“services” means anything other than goods, money and securities but includes activities relating to the use of money or its conversion by cash or by any other mode, from one form, currency or denomination, to another form, currency or denomination for which a separate consideration is charged;

For the removal of doubts, it is hereby clarified that the expression “services” includes facilitating or arranging transactions in securities. [Inserted by the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018, w.e.f. 1 February 2019]

“actionable claim” shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. [In short: a claim to an unsecured debt, or to a beneficial interest in movable property not in the claimant's possession, which civil courts recognise as a ground for relief.]
“specified actionable claim” means the actionable claim involved in or by way of betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery or online money gaming. [Inserted with effect from 1 October 2023]

entries.textNote: Definitions reproduced for study as amended to date to the best of our verification. Section 2(1) is paraphrased after its first sentence; s.2(102A) and the Explanation's insertion dates should be confirmed on the CBIC Taxinformation portal before quoting.

interpretation.h: 1. Why the two definitions matter
p: Section 9 taxes the supply of 'goods or services or both', so a transaction that is neither — money, securities, or an actionable claim protected by Schedule III — is outside the levy altogether. Classification as goods or services then decides the time of supply (ss.12 and 13), the place of supply (IGST Act ss.10 and 12/13), the rate schedule, e-way bill duties and ITC timing. Composite and mixed supplies (s.8) and the deeming entries in Schedule II settle many borderline cases before the definitions are even reached.

Structure: s.2(52) is a positive, property-based definition; s.2(102) is a residuary 'anything other than' definition. Anything that is not movable property, money or securities therefore defaults to services — rights, permissions, obligations to tolerate an act, intangibles not treated as goods.

interpretation.h: 2. 'Every kind of movable property' — tangibles and intangibles
p: The phrase is wide and borrowed from sales-tax law, so the older Supreme Court tests still guide: a thing is goods if it is capable of abstraction, consumption and use, and can be transmitted, transferred, delivered, stored or possessed. Tata Consultancy Services v. State of A.P. (SC, 2004) applied that test to hold that software recorded on a medium is goods. Under GST, however, Schedule II para 5(d) deems development, design, customisation and upgradation of IT software to be a service, and Schedule II para 1(a) treats transfer of title in goods as a supply of goods — the Schedules, not the definition alone, decide the result.

Immovable property is not goods, but things attached to land become goods when they are agreed to be severed before supply or under the contract (standing timber, crops). Electricity is treated as goods (it has a tariff heading) but is exempt.

interpretation.h: 3. Money and securities — the carve-outs and the fee rule
p: Money (s.2(75)) and securities (s.2(101), borrowing the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act meaning) are excluded from both definitions, so buying and selling them is not a supply. The services definition brings back the activity: conversion of money or currency for a separate consideration (forex margins, DD charges), and, since 1 February 2019, facilitating or arranging transactions in securities (brokerage). The test is always whether a distinct charge is made for the activity, not whether money changes hands.

interpretation.h: 4. Actionable claims: goods by definition, usually not taxed
p: Including actionable claims in 'goods' was a deliberate choice to bring lottery, betting and gambling into the levy. Skill Lotto Solutions v. Union of India (SC, 3 Dec 2020) upheld that inclusion and refused to exclude prize money from the value. Schedule III para 6, as amended with effect from 1 October 2023, then takes every other actionable claim — book debts, insurance claims, unpaid rent, receivables sold in factoring — out of GST. So the practical question is not 'is it goods?' but 'is it a specified actionable claim under s.2(102A)?'

Gameskraft (SC, 27 May 2026): the Court held online gaming platforms, including rummy and fantasy operators, are suppliers of actionable claims in betting and gambling, not mere intermediaries; whether a game is of skill or chance does not change that where stakes are placed on an uncertain outcome. Tax applies on the full value of stakes, valued under Rules 31B/31C, and the 2023 amendments were treated as clarificatory and retrospective. The Karnataka HC's 2023 order quashing the Gameskraft show-cause notice was set aside and the notice restored. Commentators (see Articles) question how this squares with the Contract Act's bar on enforcing wagers (Gherulal Parakh, SC 1959) and with the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025.

interpretation.h: 5. Vouchers — neither goods nor services
p: Advance rulings in Karnataka had treated vouchers as goods taxable at 18% (Premier Sales Promotion, AAAR 2021). The Karnataka High Court set those rulings aside in 2023, holding that vouchers are instruments for future supply — neither goods nor services — and the Madras High Court in Kalyan Jewellers (27 Nov 2023) treated a gift voucher as an actionable claim falling in Schedule III. Circular 243/37/2024-GST (31 Dec 2024) now settles the departmental position: voucher transactions are not supplies; GST applies to the underlying supply, to commission earned by agents, and to separate marketing or technology fees, but not to breakage on unredeemed vouchers.
The voucher-specific time-of-supply rules in ss.12(4)/13(4) were reported as recommended for omission by the 55th GST Council — verify whether that change has been notified before relying on it.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction with ss.7, 8 and the Schedules
p: The definitions supply the raw material; s.7 decides whether there is a supply at all and Schedules I–III re-sort transactions. Schedule II deems certain goods-like transactions to be services (transfer of right to use goods, works contracts, software development) and vice versa (transfer of title in goods is goods). Schedule III excludes actionable claims (other than specified ones), sale of land and buildings, and certain high-seas and warehoused sales. For any disputed transaction, run the order: is there a supply (s.7)? Is it deemed by Schedule II? Is it excluded by Schedule III? Only then classify under s.2(52)/2(102).

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk map
p: Disputes cluster in four places: (i) gaming, lottery and prize-based promotions after Gameskraft — expect revived demands under s.74; (ii) vouchers, wallets, loyalty points and gift cards — check Circular 243/37/2024 and the role (principal vs agent); (iii) transfers of receivables, assignment of debts and insurance claims — protected by Schedule III para 6 but often caught in audits; (iv) intangibles such as duty-credit scrips, renewable energy certificates and carbon credits, where goods-vs-services classification changes rate and place of supply. Document the legal character of each instrument in the contract.

entries.title: Charge of income-tax
entries.summary: The charging section. It levies income-tax on the total income of every person for the tax year, at the rates fixed each year by a Central Act (the Finance Act). It also covers additional income-tax, allows income of a period other than the tax year to be charged where the Act says so, and links the charge to TDS, TCS and advance tax. The wording follows 1961-Act s.4 closely, so the leading case law under that section carries over.

Not in s.4 — fixed annually by a Central Act; the Finance Act, 2026 is the first under the 2025 Act

s.4(4): income of a period other than the tax year is charged where the Act so provides
s.4(5): TDS, TCS and advance tax — TCS is now named expressly (1961 s.4(2) mentioned only TDS and advance tax)
Section 4 (same number); case law carried over — see Cases

text.t: Where any Central Act enacts that income-tax shall be charged for any tax year at any rate or rates, income-tax for such tax year shall be charged at that rate or those rates in accordance with, and subject to the provisions of, this Act.
The charge of income-tax under sub-section (1) shall be on the total income of the tax year of every person.
Income-tax shall also include any additional income-tax, by whatever name called, levied under this Act.
[Condensed] Where, by virtue of any provision of this Act, income-tax is to be charged in respect of the income of a period other than the tax year, income-tax shall be charged accordingly.
[Condensed] In respect of income chargeable under sub-section (1), income-tax shall be deducted or collected at source or paid in advance as provided under this Act.

entries.textNote: Sub-sections (2), (3) and the operative words of (1) and (5) follow the official text on incometaxindia.gov.in; sub-section (1) is partly reconstructed and (4)–(5) are condensed. Check the exact wording on the Department's section page before quoting.

interpretation.h: 1. Purpose: the charge, not the computation
p: Section 4 is the provision that actually imposes the tax. Everything else — heads of income, deductions, rates, assessment — either computes or collects what s.4 charges. It has four building blocks: (i) a Central Act fixing rates for the tax year; (ii) the person; (iii) the total income of the tax year; and (iv) the rest of the Act, which governs how the charge is applied. If any block is missing, there is no charge.

Old to new: the 1961 section charged tax 'for any assessment year' on the total income of the 'previous year'. With the tax-year concept in s.3, the 2025 Act charges tax for the tax year on the income of the same tax year. The two-year split is gone, but the logic is the same.

interpretation.h: 2. Rates come from the annual Finance Act
p: Section 4 has no rates. Each year Parliament enacts them in a Central Act, and the Finance Act, 2026 is the first to prescribe rates for tax year 2026-27 under Act 30 of 2025. The 1961-era rule from Karimtharuvi Tea Estate v. State of Kerala (SC, 1966) — that the law in force on the first day of the assessment year governs the assessment — will need re-reading for a regime with no assessment year. A reasonable view is that the rates and law in force for the tax year apply, but verify how courts settle this; no reported ruling on the point has been found yet.

Retrospective changes remain possible, but CIT v. Vatika Township (SC, Constitution Bench, 2014) holds that a substantive amendment imposing a new burden is presumed prospective unless the statute clearly says otherwise.

interpretation.h: 3. 'Total income' and the real income doctrine
p: The charge is on total income computed under the Act — not on gross receipts and not on book profit. Courts have long held that only real income is taxed: CIT v. Shoorji Vallabhdas (SC, 1962) — income given up before it accrued is not taxable; Godhra Electricity v. CIT (SC, 1997) — hypothetical income that has not materialised is not taxable; UCO Bank v. CIT (SC, 1999) — interest on doubtful loans need not be taxed on accrual; CIT v. Excel Industries (SC, 2013) — no tax on a benefit not yet usable.

Latest position: in Jindal Equipment Leasing v. CIT (SC, 9 Jan 2026) the Court restated the doctrine. Business profit can arise in kind and without a sale, but the benefit must be concrete and commercially realisable; a mere paper rearrangement is not income. Shares held as stock-in-trade and replaced by more valuable shares on amalgamation can give rise to business income where they are realisable and have a definite value. The doctrine is a guide to applying the charge, not a licence to ignore deeming provisions — State Bank of Travancore (SC, 1986) cautioned against stretching it.

interpretation.h: 4. 'Every person' and the right assessee
p: The charge falls on every person defined in the Act. Income must be taxed in the hands of the person who is legally liable for it: ITO v. Ch. Atchaiah (SC, 1996) held that the department must assess the right person and cannot choose between two persons. This matters for trusts, AOPs, firms and representative assessees, and for disputes over whose income a receipt is.

interpretation.h: 5. Other periods, additional tax and collection
p: s.4(4) carries forward the 1961 proviso: where the Act charges tax on income of a period other than the tax year — non-resident shipping, persons leaving India, discontinued businesses, AOPs formed for an event, persons likely to transfer assets to avoid tax — tax is charged on that basis. s.4(3) makes clear that additional income-tax (for example, on updated returns) is part of 'income-tax'. s.4(5) ties the charge to TDS, TCS and advance tax; naming TCS removes an old argument that collection at source rested only on the collection provisions themselves.
Because liability arises under s.4 before assessment, interest for shortfalls in advance tax and TDS defaults can be computed even before a return is filed.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction with ss.3, 5 and the transition
p: Read s.4 with s.3 (tax year), s.5 (scope of total income by residence) and s.536 (repeal and savings). For tax year 2025-26 and earlier, the 1961-Act s.4 still governs, even for returns and assessments made after 1 April 2026. The CBDT mapping utility treats the two s.4s as direct equivalents, so citations of 1961-Act s.4 cases in replies for tax year 2026-27 onwards should say so expressly.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk points
p: Common errors are applying rates to gross receipts instead of total income, treating book entries of unrealised gains as income, and assuming no liability exists until assessment. In disputes, the strongest s.4 arguments are about whether a receipt is real income at all, whether it belongs to the assessee, and which year it belongs to.

entries.title: Scope of supply
entries.chapter: Chapter III — Levy and Collection of Tax
entries.summary: The taxable event under GST. Section 7 says what counts as a supply: supplies for consideration in the course or furtherance of business, transactions between a body and its members, import of services, and the Schedule I deemed supplies made without consideration. Schedule III and notified government activities are carved out. In 2026 the live fights are on corporate guarantees (Delhi HC, 17 Nov 2026), damages and settlements (Bombay HC, Tata Sons), assignment of leasehold land (SLP dismissed) and the mutuality clause in s.7(1)(aa), which the Kerala HC struck down and the Supreme Court is now hearing.

glance.v: Defines the taxable event — no supply, no GST under s.9
s.7(1)(a) supply for consideration in course or furtherance of business; (aa) body to members; (b) import of services; (c) Schedule I without consideration
s.7(2): Schedule III and notified activities of governments and local authorities as public authorities
Corporate guarantees to group entities are a supply even without a fee; Rule 28(2) 1% value read down (Delhi HC, Sterlite Power, 17 Nov 2026)
Union's appeal against Kerala HC ruling (IMA, 2025) that struck down s.7(1)(aa) and s.2(17)(e)

text.t: For the purposes of this Act, the expression “supply” includes— (a) all forms of supply of goods or services or both such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business; (aa) the activities or transactions, by a person, other than an individual, to its members or constituents or vice-versa, for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration; (b) import of services for a consideration whether or not in the course or furtherance of business; and (c) the activities specified in Schedule I, made or agreed to be made without a consideration.

[Condensed] The person and its members or constituents are deemed to be two separate persons, and the supply of activities or transactions between them is deemed to take place from one to the other. [Clause (aa) and the Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, in force from 1 January 2022 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017; declared unconstitutional by the Kerala HC in 2025 — matter pending before the Supreme Court.]

Where certain activities or transactions constitute a supply in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (1), they shall be treated either as supply of goods or supply of services as referred to in Schedule II.

Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1),— (a) activities or transactions specified in Schedule III; or (b) such activities or transactions undertaken by the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority in which they are engaged as public authorities, as may be notified by the Government on the recommendations of the Council, shall be treated neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services.

Subject to the provisions of sub-sections (1), (1A) and (2), the Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, specify, by notification, the transactions that are to be treated as— (a) a supply of goods and not as a supply of services; or (b) a supply of services and not as a supply of goods.

entries.textNote: Text reproduced for study as amended to date to the best of our verification. The Explanation to clause (aa) is condensed; former clause (d) (Schedule II) was omitted and replaced by sub-section (1A) by the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018, retrospectively from 1 July 2017. Confirm the wording on the CBIC Taxinformation portal before quoting.

interpretation.h: 1. Why s.7 is the gateway
p: Section 9 levies tax on intra-State supplies, so every demand starts with s.7. If a transaction is not a supply — or is pulled out by s.7(2) — there is nothing to tax, no invoice to issue and no time or place of supply to fix. The word includes makes the definition inclusive: the forms listed in clause (a) (sale, transfer, barter, licence, lease and so on) are examples, not a closed list.

Order of analysis: (i) is there a supply under s.7(1)? (ii) is it excluded by Schedule III or a s.7(2)(b) notification? (iii) does Schedule II classify it as goods or services (s.7(1A))? (iv) is it composite or mixed (s.8)? Only then turn to rate, value (s.15) and place of supply.

interpretation.h: 2. Clause (a): consideration + business
p: Clause (a) has three ingredients: a supply of goods or services, for a consideration (s.2(31)), and in the course or furtherance of business (s.2(17)). Consideration requires a link between the payment and the supply — a quid pro quo. CBIC's Circular 178/10/2022-GST says liquidated damages, forfeitures, late-payment charges and similar compensation are generally not consideration unless they are really the price of tolerating an act.

The Bombay HC applied that reasoning in Tata Sons v. Union of India (reported Aug 2026): settling an arbitral award with NTT Docomo was not a supply, and Schedule II entry 5(e) ('agreeing to tolerate an act') cannot create a levy where there is no independent agreement supported by consideration. The Kerala HC similarly held that penalties imposed by an oil company on its distributors were not consideration (Aswathy Gas Agencies, 2025).

Business: s.2(17) is wide, but the transaction must still be in its course or furtherance. In Aerocom Cushions (Bom HC, Nagpur, 9 Jan 2026) assignment of leasehold rights in an MIDC plot with building was held to be a transfer of immovable property, not a supply of service; the Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue's SLP in 2026. Gujarat HC rulings in 2025 (Time Technoplast, Life Sciences Chemicals) reached the same result by treating such assignments as akin to sale of land under Schedule III entry 5.

interpretation.h: 3. Clause (aa): clubs, associations and the mutuality fight
p: Before GST, State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club (SC, 3-judge bench, 3 Oct 2019) held that a members' club and its members are not two persons, so there is no sale or service between them (doctrine of mutuality). Parliament responded with clause (aa) and the deeming Explanation through the Finance Act, 2021, retrospectively from 1 July 2017.

The Kerala HC Division Bench in Indian Medical Association v. Union of India (2025:KER:30517, April 2025) held clause (aa), s.2(17)(e) and the Explanation unconstitutional for want of legislative competence: Article 246A permits a tax on supply, and a transaction with oneself is not a supply. The Union's appeal is pending before the Supreme Court, which issued notice in July 2025 and directed no coercive recovery against IMA for the past period. Status: Pending — verify the next hearing. Outside Kerala, clause (aa) remains on the statute book; plead the Kerala ruling as persuasive and keep the issue alive in replies.

interpretation.h: 4. Clause (c) and Schedule I: supply without consideration
p: Schedule I deems four kinds of transactions to be supplies even without consideration: (1) permanent transfer or disposal of business assets where ITC was availed; (2) supplies between related persons or distinct persons (s.25) in the course or furtherance of business, with gifts to employees up to ₹50,000 a year excluded; (3) principal–agent supplies of goods; (4) import of services from a related person or own establishment outside India in the course or furtherance of business.

Corporate guarantees. Rule 28(2), inserted by Notification 52/2023-CT (26 Oct 2023), valued a guarantee to a related person at 1% of the guaranteed amount a year, and Circular 204/16/2023-GST clarified its application. In Sterlite Power Transmission v. Union of India (Delhi HC, Division Bench, reported 17 Nov 2026) the Court held that a guarantee by a holding or group company for a related entity's loan is a supply of service under Schedule I entry 2 even when no fee is charged, with the borrowing group company as recipient. It distinguished the service-tax decision in Edelweiss Financial Services (SC, 2023) and read down the 1% value so that it is not a fixed floor: a lower open-market value can be shown with verifiable evidence. Expect an appeal; verify status.

Distinct persons. Circular 199/11/2023-GST accepts that where the recipient branch is eligible for full ITC, the value declared on the invoice (even nil) may be treated as open-market value under the second proviso to Rule 28(1); the Delhi HC applied this in KEI Industries (2025) to set aside an IGST demand on head-office services without cross-charge.

interpretation.h: 5. Clause (b): import of services
p: Import of services for consideration is a supply even if not for business — which is why individuals and charities importing services can be liable under reverse charge. Where there is no consideration, only Schedule I entry 4 (related person or own foreign establishment, in the course of business) brings it in. Circular 210/4/2024-GST says that where the recipient is entitled to full ITC, the invoice value (or nil, if no invoice) can be taken as the open-market value for related-party imports. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (SC, 19 May 2022) the Court held that ocean freight in a CIF import is part of a composite supply of goods and cannot be taxed again as a separate import of service.

interpretation.h: 6. Section 7(2) and Schedule III: what is not a supply
p: Schedule III removes, among others: employee services to the employer; court and tribunal functions; duties of MPs, MLAs and constitutional office-holders; funeral services; sale of land and (subject to Schedule II para 5(b)) of completed buildings; actionable claims other than specified ones; high-seas sales, warehoused sales before home clearance, and merchant-trading out-and-out sales. Circular 172/04/2022-GST says perquisites given to employees under the employment contract are not supplies.

Section 7(2)(b) works through Notification 14/2017-Central Tax (Rate): only the activities notified there (largely constitutional functions of panchayats and municipalities) are excluded. Other services by governments are supplies, often exempt or taxable under reverse charge.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk map
p: Recurring s.7 disputes: (i) guarantees, cross-charges and secondments within groups — document the arrangement and valuation, and after Sterlite Power keep evidence for any value below 1%; (ii) settlements, damages and termination payments — draft the agreement to show compensation for loss, not a price for tolerating an act; (iii) land and leasehold transfers — rely on Schedule III entry 5 and the Aerocom Cushions SLP dismissal; (iv) clubs, RWAs and associations — preserve the mutuality challenge pending the Supreme Court; (v) asset disposals and free supplies to related parties — Schedule I applies only where ITC was taken or the parties are related or distinct.

entries.title: Scope of total income
entries.old1961: Section 5, Income-tax Act, 1961 (scope of total income), with Explanations 1 and 2
entries.summary: Section 5 tells you which income of a person enters total income, depending on residential status. A resident is taxed on worldwide income; a not-ordinarily-resident on Indian income plus foreign income from a business controlled or profession set up in India; a non-resident only on income received or accruing in India. The 2025 Act keeps the substance of 1961-Act s.5 and turns its proviso and Explanations into clauses and sub-sections, so the 1961 case law carries over.

glance.v: Fixes the reach of the s.4 charge by residential status (s.6)
Worldwide income — received in India, accruing in India, or accruing outside India
Indian receipts and accruals; foreign income only if from a business controlled in, or profession set up in, India — s.6(13) defines NOR
Only income received or deemed received in India, or accruing or deemed to accrue in India (s.9)
s.5(3): balance-sheet entry in India is not receipt; s.5(4): no double inclusion on accrual and later receipt
s.5 (same number); proviso → clause (c); Explanations 1–2 → s.5(3)–(4); case law carried over

text.t: [In substance] Subject to the provisions of this Act, the total income of any tax year of a person who is resident includes all income from whatever source derived which— (a) is received or is deemed to be received in India in that tax year by or on behalf of such person; (b) accrues or arises or is deemed to accrue or arise to him in India during that tax year; or (c) accrues or arises to him outside India during that tax year — but, for a person not ordinarily resident in India under section 6(13), income accruing or arising outside India is included only if it is derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India.

[In substance] Subject to the provisions of this Act, the total income of any tax year of a person who is a non-resident includes all income from whatever source derived which— (a) is received or is deemed to be received in India in that tax year by or on behalf of such person; or (b) accrues or arises or is deemed to accrue or arise to him in India during that tax year.
[In substance] Income accruing or arising outside India shall not be deemed to be received in India by reason only of the fact that it is taken into account in a balance sheet prepared in India.

[In substance] Income included in total income on the basis that it has accrued or arisen, or is deemed to have accrued or arisen, shall not again be included on the basis that it is received or deemed to be received in India.

entries.textNote: The official text on incometaxindia.gov.in was consulted, but the wording above is reproduced in substance, not verbatim: the structure and cross-reference to s.6(13) are confirmed, while the exact drafting should be checked on the Department's section page before quoting.

interpretation.h: 1. Purpose: the territorial reach of the charge
p: Section 4 charges tax on total income; s.5 says what that total income contains for each class of person. It works with s.6 (residence) and s.9 (income deemed to accrue in India). The three connecting factors — receipt in India, accrual in India and accrual outside India — are the same as in the 1961 Act, and the CBDT mapping treats the two sections as direct equivalents.

What changed in drafting: the NOR proviso to 1961-Act s.5(1) now sits inside clause (c) of s.5(1); the NOR definition moves from s.6(6) to s.6(13); Explanation 1 (balance sheet) becomes s.5(3) and Explanation 2 (no double counting) becomes s.5(4). Commentators note no change in substance.

interpretation.h: 2. Receipt: the first receipt rule
p: 'Received in India' means the first occasion on which the assessee obtains the money as his own. Once received abroad, a later remittance to India is not a fresh receipt — a rule settled under the 1961 Act in Keshav Mills v. CIT (SC, 1953) and applied repeatedly since. This 1961-Act precedent is carried over because the wording is the same in substance.

2026 application: in Kaushal Ganpatbhai Patel v. ITO (ITAT Ahmedabad, 9 Feb 2026) salary of a non-resident employed by a Seychelles company, for services rendered outside India, was held not taxable merely because it was credited to his NRE account in India. Revenue often relies on such credits; the answer is to show where the employer discharged the obligation and where the services were rendered.

interpretation.h: 3. Accrual: right to receive and territorial nexus
p: Income accrues when the assessee acquires a right to receive it, even if payment comes later (E.D. Sassoon & Co. v. CIT, SC 1954). Accrual 'in India' needs a territorial nexus; for non-residents s.9 supplies deemed nexus for business connection, property, salary for services in India, interest, royalty and fees for technical services. In Ishikawajima-Harima Heavy Industries v. DIT (SC, 2007) the Court held that offshore supplies and services did not accrue in India merely because the project was in India.

Pride Foramer S.A. v. CIT (SC, Oct 2025) — non-resident drilling company: a non-resident need not have a permanent establishment or office in India for income from a business connection to be taxable under ss.5(2) and 9(1)(i); PE matters only for treaty relief.

Teva Pharmaceuticals v. Revenue (Delhi HC, 15 Sep 2026): a payment by an Indian resident to a non-resident does not by itself mean income accrues in India; s.9's deemed-accrual heads are specific and cannot be widened into a 'payer rule'. Reassessment notices founded on that premise were quashed. Based on reports — verify against the certified copy.

interpretation.h: 4. The two safeguards in s.5(3) and s.5(4)
p: Balance sheet rule (s.5(3)). Foreign income is not 'received in India' merely because it appears in accounts or a balance sheet prepared in India. The related 1961 principle in CIT v. Toshoku Ltd. (SC, 1980): a book credit in an Indian payer's accounts in favour of a non-resident is not receipt by the non-resident in India.

No double counting (s.5(4)). Once income has been taxed on accrual, its later receipt in India is not taxed again. This protects residents taxed on foreign accruals who later remit the money, and assessees who have been taxed on a mercantile basis.

interpretation.h: 5. The NOR band
p: A not-ordinarily-resident person pays tax like a resident on Indian income but, for foreign income, only on income from a business controlled in India or a profession set up in India. The category now includes, under s.6(13) of the 2025 Act, the 'deemed resident' Indian citizen and high-income visitors who become resident under the 120-day rule — so a returning NRI or a citizen not taxed anywhere else should check NOR status before reporting worldwide income. Whether control of a business is 'in India' is a question of where the head and brain sit, not where operations run.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction and transition
p: Read s.5 with s.6 (residence, studied next in the queue), s.9 (deemed accrual), the DTAA provisions (which can relieve tax even where s.5 includes income) and s.536 (transition). For FY 2025-26 and earlier, 1961-Act s.5 still applies. Because the 2025 Act also changes some drafting in s.9, check the specific deemed-accrual clause rather than relying only on 1961-era section numbers.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk points
p: Common audit issues: NRE/NRO credits treated as receipts; payments by Indian companies to foreign vendors assumed to be Indian income; returning NRIs reporting or omitting foreign income without checking NOR status; foreign income taxed twice on accrual and on remittance. Keep employment contracts, invoices, place-of-service evidence and remittance trails, and match residential-status workings to s.6 every year.

Do not tax income twice on accrual and on later remittance (s.5(4)); keep the trail.
When citing 1961-Act s.5 cases for tax year 2026-27 onwards, say expressly that the provision is carried over.

entries.title: Levy and collection
entries.chapter: Chapter III — Levy and Collection of Tax
entries.summary: The charging section of the CGST Act. Section 9(1) levies central tax on every intra-State supply, on the value under s.15, at notified rates capped at 20%. It keeps alcoholic liquor for human consumption (and, since 1 Nov 2024, ENA and rectified spirit used to make it) outside GST, and holds the five petroleum products in suspense under s.9(2). Sub-sections (3) to (5) move the duty to pay away from the supplier — to the recipient under reverse charge, or to the e-commerce operator. From 1 Nov 2026 reverse charge was widened to scrap and used cooking oil, and the e-commerce entry for local delivery became a wider 'delivery services' entry at 5% without ITC.

glance.v: Creates the CGST levy on intra-State supplies and decides who must pay it
Up to 20% CGST, notified on Council recommendation (matching SGST gives the 40% top slab)
Alcoholic liquor for human consumption; ENA / rectified spirit for making it (from 1 Nov 2024)
Crude, petrol, diesel, natural gas and ATF — no date notified under s.9(2)
s.9(3) RCM by notified category; s.9(4) RCM by class of registered recipient buying from unregistered suppliers; s.9(5) e-commerce operator pays
RCM on plastic, tyre and e-waste scrap and used cooking oil (Notf. 04/2026-CT(R)); s.9(5) 'delivery services' at 5% without ITC (Notf. 06 & 09/2026-CT(R)), all from 1 Nov 2026

text.t: Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), there shall be levied a tax called the central goods and services tax on all intra-State supplies of goods or services or both, except on the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption and un-denatured extra neutral alcohol or rectified spirit used for manufacture of alcoholic liquor, for human consumption, on the value determined under section 15 and at such rates, not exceeding twenty per cent., as may be notified by the Government on the recommendations of the Council and collected in such manner as may be prescribed and shall be paid by the taxable person.

The central tax on the supply of petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (commonly known as petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel shall be levied with effect from such date as may be notified by the Government on the recommendations of the Council.

The Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, by notification, specify categories of supply of goods or services or both, the tax on which shall be paid on reverse charge basis by the recipient of such goods or services or both and all the provisions of this Act shall apply to such recipient as if he is the person liable for paying the tax in relation to the supply of such goods or services or both.

The Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, by notification, specify a class of registered persons who shall, in respect of supply of specified categories of goods or services or both received from an unregistered supplier, pay the tax on reverse charge basis as the recipient of such supply of goods or services or both, and all the provisions of this Act shall apply to such recipient as if he is the person liable for paying the tax in relation to such supply of goods or services or both.

The Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, by notification, specify categories of services the tax on intra-State supplies of which shall be paid by the electronic commerce operator if such services are supplied through it, and all the provisions of this Act shall apply to such electronic commerce operator as if he is the supplier liable for paying the tax in relation to the supply of such services.

[Condensed] Where the e-commerce operator has no physical presence in the taxable territory, any person representing it there is liable to pay the tax; if it has neither presence nor a representative, it must appoint a person in the taxable territory to pay the tax, and that person is liable.

entries.textNote: Text reproduced for study as amended to date to the best of our verification. The ENA / rectified-spirit words in s.9(1) were inserted by s.114 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, effective 1 November 2024 (Notification 17/2024-Central Tax). Sub-section (4) is shown in the form substituted by the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 (from 1 Feb 2019); the provisos to sub-section (5) are condensed. Confirm the current wording on the CBIC Taxinformation portal before quoting.

interpretation.h: 1. Purpose: the levy, the rate ceiling and the person who pays
p: Section 9 is to the CGST Act what s.4 is to the Income-tax Act: it creates the tax. Every other provision computes it (s.15 value, ss.12–13 time of supply), collects it (ss.39, 49) or recovers it (ss.73–74A). Its five elements are (i) an intra-State supply — inter-State supplies are taxed under s.5 of the IGST Act; (ii) a supply within s.7, studied on 25 Nov 2026; (iii) value under s.15; (iv) a rate notified on the Council's recommendation; and (v) the person liable — the taxable person by default, or the recipient or e-commerce operator where sub-sections (3) to (5) apply.

The 20% ceiling is a real limit: notified CGST rates must stay within it. After the September 2025 rate rationalisation (Notification 09/2025-Central Tax (Rate), effective 22 Sep 2025) the slabs became 5%, 18% and a 40% special rate; 40% is 20% CGST plus 20% SGST, so the top slab sits exactly at the statutory ceiling. A further increase would need an amendment to s.9(1).

interpretation.h: 2. What s.9(1) leaves out: alcohol and ENA
p: Article 366(12A) of the Constitution defines GST to exclude alcoholic liquor for human consumption, and s.9(1) mirrors that. The fight was over extra neutral alcohol (ENA) and rectified spirit — inputs for potable liquor that are not themselves fit to drink. In State of U.P. v. Lalta Prasad Vaish (SC, 9-judge bench, 23 Oct 2024) the majority held that 'intoxicating liquor' in Entry 8 of List II covers industrial alcohol as well, partly departing from Synthetics & Chemicals (1990) and strengthening the States' hand.

Parliament had already acted: s.114 of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 added ENA and rectified spirit used to make potable liquor to the s.9(1) exclusion from 1 Nov 2024. Commentators read the change as prospective, so pre-November 2024 disputes over whether GST or State VAT applied remain open. The Bombay HC at Goa (United Spirits, 23 Dec 2025) refused to waive VAT interest for FY 2019-20 on the ground of that uncertainty — a reminder that paying under protest to one regime does not settle the other.

interpretation.h: 3. Section 9(2): petroleum in suspense
p: The five petroleum products are within GST in law but the levy has not started, because no date has been notified. Until it is, they bear central excise and State VAT, and GST charged on inputs used to make or sell them cannot be credited against those taxes. For oil, gas and aviation businesses this blocked credit is a permanent cost; s.17(2) apportionment treats those outward supplies as non-taxable.

interpretation.h: 4. Reverse charge under s.9(3) and s.9(4)
p: s.9(3) works by category of supply: Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) lists services (GTA, legal services by advocates, security services, sponsorship, director's services, renting of commercial property by an unregistered person to a registered person from 10 Oct 2024, and others) and Notification 4/2017-Central Tax (Rate) lists goods. From 1 Nov 2026 Notification 04/2026-Central Tax (Rate) added used cooking oil and waste and scrap of plastics, tyres and electrical/electronic items supplied by unregistered persons to registered persons. s.9(4) works by class of recipient: since the 2019 substitution it applies only to notified registered persons buying notified items from unregistered suppliers — mainly real-estate promoters under Notification 07/2019-Central Tax (Rate).

The deeming words 'as if he is the person liable' put the recipient in the supplier's place for every purpose — registration (s.24 requires it regardless of threshold), payment in cash (s.49(4) read with s.2(82) bars use of the credit ledger for RCM tax), self-invoicing (s.31(3)(f)) and interest and penalty. The recipient can then take ITC of the RCM tax, subject to ss.16–17.

Limits on the power: in Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (SC, 19 May 2022) the Court struck down IGST under reverse charge on ocean freight in CIF imports, because the importer had already paid tax on the composite supply of goods; it also held that GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding. Challenges by suppliers whose own output moved to reverse charge and who lose the use of their input credit have failed: Eagle Security & Personnel Services (Bom HC, 2025) upheld the security-services notifications against Articles 14 and 19(1)(g).

interpretation.h: 5. E-commerce operators under s.9(5)
p: Section 9(5) treats the operator as the supplier for notified services supplied 'through it'. Notification 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) covers passenger transport by motor vehicle, accommodation, housekeeping (such as plumbing and carpentry), restaurant services (from 1 Jan 2022) and, from 22 Sep 2025, local delivery. From 1 Nov 2026 Notification 09/2026-Central Tax (Rate) replaced that entry with 'delivery services, other than postal and courier services', for providers not liable to register, and Notification 06/2026-Central Tax (Rate) set 5% without ITC for them. Expect questions on where 'delivery' ends and courier or GTA begins.

The key word is through. Platforms on a flat subscription model argue they only license software. Advance rulings in Karnataka have split, treating some aggregators as liable under s.9(5) and some subscription-model apps as outside it, according to how far the platform controls booking, fare and tracking. No binding court ruling settles the test yet — verify before advising a platform client. The operator pays from its cash ledger and the actual provider reports the supply as one on which the operator pays.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction with other sections
p: Read s.9 with s.7 (no supply, no levy), s.15 (value), ss.12–13 (time of supply; for RCM services, the earliest of payment or 60 days from the supplier's invoice), s.22 and s.24 (registration), s.31(3)(f)–(g) (self-invoice and payment voucher), s.49(4) (no ITC for paying RCM tax), s.10 (composition dealers must still pay RCM in cash) and s.51 (2% GST TDS on specified scrap purchases from 1 Nov 2026, which sits alongside RCM). For inter-State supplies the same structure is in ss.5(3)–(5) of the IGST Act.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk map
p: Most s.9 demands come from: (i) RCM missed on recurring items — GTA, legal fees, directors' sitting fees, security, rent from unregistered landlords; (ii) composition dealers and small recipients who forget that RCM applies to them; (iii) RCM paid from the credit ledger, which is not a valid payment; (iv) scrap buyers after 1 Nov 2026 who must now apply RCM, check suppliers' registration and deduct GST TDS; and (v) platforms unsure whether they supply 'through' themselves. Build an RCM matrix by vendor type and HSN/SAC and reconcile it with GSTR-3B Table 3.1(d) every month.

entries.title: Residence in India
entries.old1961: Section 6, Income-tax Act, 1961 (residence in India), including s.6(1A) deemed residence and s.6(6) not ordinarily resident
entries.summary: Section 6 decides residential status for each tax year, and through s.5 that decides how much income India taxes. Individuals are tested on days in India (182 days, or 60 days plus 365 in the four earlier years), with relaxations for citizens leaving for work or for visitors, a 120-day rule for high earners and a deemed-residence rule for stateless-for-tax citizens. HUFs, firms and AOPs turn on control and management, companies on Indian incorporation or place of effective management. The 2025 Act keeps the 1961 tests and only renumbers them, so the 1961 case law — including the 2026 Binny Bansal ruling — carries over.

glance.v: 182 days or more in the tax year, or 60 days plus 365 days in the four preceding tax years (s.6(2))

60-day test does not apply to citizens leaving for employment or as Indian-ship crew, or to citizens/PIOs visiting India (s.6(3)–(4)); becomes 120 days for visitors with Indian income over ₹15 lakh (s.6(5))

text.t: [In substance] The residential status of a person in a tax year is determined under this section.

[In substance] An individual is resident in India in a tax year if he is in India (a) for a period or periods amounting in all to 182 days or more in that tax year; or (b) for 60 days or more in that tax year and 365 days or more in the four preceding tax years.

[Condensed] Clause (2)(b) does not apply to an Indian citizen who leaves India in the tax year as a member of the crew of an Indian ship or for employment outside India (s.6(3)), or, subject to s.6(5), to an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin who comes on a visit to India (s.6(4)). For such a visitor whose total income, other than income from foreign sources, exceeds ₹15 lakh, the 60 days in clause (2)(b) is read as 120 days (s.6(5)). For crew of a foreign-bound ship, days in India are counted as prescribed (s.6(6)).

[Condensed] An Indian citizen whose total income, other than income from foreign sources, exceeds ₹15 lakh is deemed resident in a tax year if he is not liable to tax in any other country by reason of domicile, residence or similar criteria; this does not apply to an individual already resident under sub-sections (2) to (6).

[Condensed] A Hindu undivided family, firm or association of persons is resident unless control and management of its affairs is situated wholly outside India in the tax year (s.6(9)). A company is resident if it is an Indian company or its place of effective management — the place where key management and commercial decisions necessary for the business as a whole are in substance made — is in India in that year (s.6(10)). Every other person is resident unless control and management is wholly outside India (s.6(11)). A person resident for any source of income in a tax year is resident for all other sources in that year (s.6(12)).

[Condensed] A person is not ordinarily resident in a tax year if (a) an individual, or the manager of an HUF, who has been non-resident in nine out of ten preceding tax years or in India for 729 days or less in the seven preceding tax years; (b) a citizen or person of Indian origin with income (other than from foreign sources) over ₹15 lakh who is resident only because of 120 to 181 days' stay; or (c) a citizen deemed resident under sub-section (7). 'Income from foreign sources' means income accruing or arising outside India (other than from a business controlled in or profession set up in India) that is not deemed to accrue or arise in India (s.6(14)).

entries.textNote: Sub-sections (2) to (14) are condensed or given in substance from secondary reproductions of the Act (CAclubindia, EZTax) and the mapping in the TaxGuru article listed below; the official section page could not be loaded during this run. Check the exact wording on incometaxindia.gov.in before quoting. We found no Finance Act, 2026 change to s.6 — verify.

interpretation.h: 1. Purpose: residence decides the reach of s.5
p: Residence is fixed separately for each tax year, and once fixed it decides which income enters total income under s.5 (studied on 25 Nov 2026): a resident and ordinarily resident is taxed on worldwide income, a not-ordinarily-resident on Indian income plus foreign income from a business controlled or profession set up in India, and a non-resident only on income received or accruing in India. Citizenship is generally irrelevant — except in the visitor, employment and deemed-residence rules, which apply only to citizens or persons of Indian origin.

Old to new: the 2025 Act keeps every 1961 test and moves them into numbered sub-sections — Explanation 1 to old s.6(1) becomes s.6(3)–(6), deemed residence moves from s.6(1A) to s.6(7)–(8), NOR from s.6(6) to s.6(13), and 'income from foreign sources' becomes s.6(14). Because the substance is unchanged, 1961-Act precedents are carried over below, and we say so for each.

interpretation.h: 2. The day-count tests for individuals
p: Presence in India counts whether or not the stay is continuous or the person intends to stay. Two questions keep returning. Part days: the Act has no rule on arrival and departure days. Rulings differ; a Delhi ITAT order reported in November 2026 (case name not yet published) excluded the arrival day by applying s.9 of the General Clauses Act and so brought a taxpayer below 182 days for three years — verify the order before relying on it. Keep passport stamps and travel records either way. Involuntary stay: in CIT v. Suresh Nanda (Delhi HC, 27 May 2015, under the 1961 Act, carried over) days spent in India only because the passport was illegally impounded were excluded. CBDT Circular 11/2020 gave Covid-related relief for FY 2019-20 only, and Circular 2/2021 declined a general relaxation for later years.

Seafarers: ITAT Jaipur in Mahesh Dadhich v. ITO (order reported 26 Oct 2026, AY 2015-16, 1961 Act, carried over) held an Indian citizen working on foreign ships to be non-resident where he was in India for fewer than 182 days, rejecting the AO's use of the 60-day plus 365-day test; his salary for service outside India was not taxable.

interpretation.h: 3. Leaving India for employment and visiting India
p: Section 6(3) — 'leaves India for the purposes of employment outside India' — switches off the 60-day test in the year of departure. The 1961 case law, carried over, reads 'employment' broadly to include taking up work or business abroad (CIT v. Avtar Singh Wadhwan, Bom HC, 2001). Section 6(4) protects citizens and PIOs coming on a visit.

Latest position: the Bangalore ITAT in Binny Bansal (9 Jan 2026, 1961 Act, carried over) held that the visitor relief helps a person who is already non-resident and visits India, not someone who was resident in the earlier years, moved abroad and then visited; and the employment relief failed because he had left India in an earlier financial year. Found resident under the Act and under the India–Singapore treaty tie-breaker (permanent home and centre of vital interests in India), his capital gains of about ₹162.5 crore were taxable in India. Plan departures so that the year of leaving is the year the employment relief is claimed, and keep evidence of the foreign home and economic ties for the treaty test.

interpretation.h: 4. The ₹15 lakh rules: 120 days and deemed residence
p: Introduced by the Finance Act, 2020 (from AY 2021-22) and carried into s.6(5) and s.6(7), these target high-income Indians who spread their time across countries. A visiting citizen or PIO with Indian income above ₹15 lakh becomes resident on 120 days plus 365 days in the four earlier years; a citizen with such income who is not liable to tax anywhere else by domicile or residence is deemed resident without any day count. Both outcomes are NOR under s.6(13)(b)–(c), so foreign income stays outside the net unless it comes from a business controlled or profession set up in India.

'Liable to tax' is the weak point. A person living in a country with no personal income tax may still be liable to tax there in principle; the treaty-law debate on whether that is enough has not been settled for s.6(7) by any reported court ruling we found — verify before advising, and keep a tax residency certificate where one is available.

interpretation.h: 5. HUFs, firms, AOPs and companies
p: For HUFs, firms and AOPs the test is control and management — the head and brain that direct the affairs, not where day-to-day operations happen (V.V.R.N.M. Subbayya Chettiar v. CIT, SC, 1950, carried over). Residence is the default: the entity is non-resident only if control and management is wholly outside India.

A company is resident if it is an Indian company or its place of effective management (POEM) is in India. CBDT Circular 6/2017 sets out the guiding principles — active business outside India, where the board actually makes decisions, and where senior management functions in substance — and Circular 8/2017 keeps companies with turnover of ₹50 crore or less outside the POEM test. These circulars were issued under the 1961 Act; check whether they have been re-issued or saved under s.536 before citing them for tax year 2026-27 onwards.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction with ss.5, 9, DTAAs and the transition
p: Residence feeds s.5 (scope), s.9 (deemed accrual for non-residents), the NOR band, and many other provisions — TDS on payments to non-residents, foreign-asset reporting, and treaty relief. Where a person is resident in India and in another country, the treaty tie-breaker (permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality) decides residence for treaty purposes only; domestic status under s.6 is unchanged. For FY 2025-26 and earlier, 1961-Act s.6 continues to apply under s.536.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk points
p: Common errors: counting days from memory instead of passport or immigration records; assuming the 182-day rule is the only test; claiming the visitor relief after moving abroad (Binny Bansal); missing the ₹15 lakh 120-day rule for frequent visitors; filing as non-resident when the person is NOR, or vice versa; treating an offshore company as non-resident while its board meets or decides in India. Prepare a year-by-year residence working, covering at least the last ten tax years for NOR, and keep it on file with the return.
