entries.title: Composition levy
entries.chapter: Chapter III — Levy and Collection of Tax
entries.summary: The optional simplified scheme for small taxpayers. Instead of tax under s.9(1), an eligible registered person pays a flat percentage of turnover — 1% for manufacturers and traders, 5% for restaurants, and 6% under the separate s.10(2A) scheme for service providers and mixed suppliers — but cannot collect tax, claim input tax credit or make inter-State supplies. The option lapses automatically once the turnover limit is crossed, and ineligible use attracts tax plus penalty under s.10(5). In 2026 the GST portal split the s.10(1) and s.10(2A) categories (from 1 Nov 2026), and GSTAT benches have confirmed the automatic lapse while allowing tax-inclusive (Rule 35) valuation after it.

glance.v: Registered person with aggregate turnover in the preceding FY up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in notified special category States) under s.10(1); up to ₹50 lakh under s.10(2A)
Manufacturers 1%, traders and other suppliers 1% of taxable turnover, restaurant service 5% (Rule 7); s.10(2A) service / mixed suppliers 6%

No inter-State outward supply, no non-taxable supply, no services through a TCS-collecting e-commerce operator, no notified goods (ice cream, pan masala, tobacco, aerated water, bricks and tiles), no casual or non-resident persons
No tax collected from buyers and no ITC (s.10(4)); bill of supply instead of tax invoice; reverse charge still payable in cash
Automatic lapse on crossing the limit with Rule 35 cum-tax relief (GSTAT Hyderabad and Dehradun); paper-only CMP-05/07 denials; separate s.10(2A) category on the portal from 1 Nov 2026

text.t: [In substance] Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Act but subject to sub-sections (3) and (4) of section 9, a registered person whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year did not exceed fifty lakh rupees may opt to pay, in lieu of the tax payable by him under sub-section (1) of section 9, an amount of tax calculated at such rate as may be prescribed, but not exceeding— (a) one per cent. of the turnover in State or Union territory in the case of a manufacturer; (b) two and a half per cent. of the turnover in State or Union territory in the case of persons engaged in making supplies referred to in clause (b) of paragraph 6 of Schedule II; and (c) half per cent. of the turnover in State or Union territory in the case of other suppliers.

[Condensed] The Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, raise the turnover limit up to ₹1.5 crore (done from 1 April 2019 by Notification 14/2019-CT). A person may opt even though he supplies services (other than restaurant-type supplies) of a value up to 10% of turnover in the State or Union territory in the preceding year or ₹5 lakh, whichever is higher. The value of exempt services by way of deposits, loans or advances, where the consideration is interest or discount, is ignored for eligibility.

[Condensed] A registered person is eligible under sub-section (1) only if he is not engaged in the supply of services (except as allowed above); not engaged in any supply of goods or services not leviable to tax under this Act; not engaged in making inter-State outward supplies; not engaged in making any supply of services through an electronic commerce operator required to collect tax at source under section 52 (goods were removed from this bar from 1 October 2023); not a manufacturer of notified goods; and is neither a casual taxable person nor a non-resident taxable person. Where more than one registered person has the same PAN, none can opt unless all opt.

[Condensed] A registered person not eligible under sub-sections (1) and (2), whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year did not exceed ₹50 lakh, may opt to pay tax at a prescribed rate not exceeding 3% of turnover in the State or Union territory, subject to the same exclusions (non-taxable supplies, inter-State outward supplies, services through a TCS-collecting e-commerce operator, casual or non-resident persons, notified goods) and the same-PAN rule. [Inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019, from 1 January 2020]

The option availed of by a registered person under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2A) shall lapse with effect from the day on which his aggregate turnover during a financial year exceeds the limit specified under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2A).

A taxable person to whom the provisions of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2A) apply shall not collect any tax from the recipient on supplies made by him nor shall he be entitled to any credit of input tax.

[In substance] If the proper officer has reasons to believe that a taxable person has paid tax under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2A) despite not being eligible, such person shall, in addition to any tax that may be payable by him under any other provisions of this Act, be liable to a penalty, and the provisions of section 73 or section 74 or section 74A shall, mutatis mutandis, apply for determination of tax and penalty.

[Condensed] For eligibility, aggregate turnover includes supplies from 1 April of the year up to the date the person becomes liable to register, and excludes exempt interest or discount on deposits, loans or advances. For computing the tax payable, 'turnover in State or Union territory' also excludes that exempt interest or discount.

entries.textNote: Sub-sections (3) and (4) follow the official text; the rest is given in substance or condensed from the CBIC Taxinformation version (amended by the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018, the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019, the Finance Acts of 2020 and 2023, and the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, which added s.74A to s.10(5)). The statutory ceilings in s.10(1) and (2A) are CGST-only; Rule 7 and Notification 2/2019-CT(R) set the actual rates, matched by SGST. Confirm the exact wording on the CBIC portal before quoting.

interpretation.h: 1. Purpose: a turnover tax in place of the value-added chain
p: Section 10 lets small businesses step outside the credit chain: they pay a small percentage of turnover instead of tax on value under s.9(1), file one quarterly payment statement (CMP-08) and one annual return (GSTR-4), and keep simpler records. The price is that the chain breaks at them — they cannot collect tax from buyers or take ITC (s.10(4)), so registered buyers get no credit on their purchases. That is why the scheme suits sellers to consumers far better than sellers to businesses.

Two schemes, not one. s.10(1) is the original scheme for manufacturers, traders and restaurants (turnover up to ₹1.5 crore). s.10(2A), added from 1 January 2020, is a separate scheme at 6% for service providers and mixed suppliers who cannot use s.10(1) (turnover up to ₹50 lakh). From 1 November 2026 the GST portal treats them as mutually exclusive categories — a person can tick several s.10(1) categories but only the single s.10(2A) category, and must keep the same category across all GSTINs under one PAN (GSTN advisory, 1 Nov 2026; Rule 19 as substituted by Notification 05/2026-CT).

interpretation.h: 2. Eligibility: the turnover test and the exclusions
p: Turnover. The test is aggregate turnover (s.2(6)) of the preceding financial year on an all-India PAN basis, not turnover of one State. It covers taxable, exempt and export supplies and inter-State supplies between distinct persons, but excludes tax and inward reverse-charge supplies. Exempt interest or discount on deposits and loans is ignored, so a trader earning bank interest is not pushed out. Notified special category States use ₹75 lakh instead of ₹1.5 crore (Notification 14/2019-CT).

Exclusions. The bar on inter-State outward supply is absolute — even a single inter-State sale breaches s.10(2). Since 1 October 2023 (Finance Act, 2023 and Notification 36/2023-CT), a composition dealer may sell goods through an e-commerce operator within the State, and the operator must block inter-State orders; supplying services through a TCS-collecting operator still disqualifies. Manufacturers of notified goods are out: ice cream and edible ice, pan masala and tobacco (Notification 8/2017-CT, carried into 14/2019-CT), aerated water (Notification 43/2019-CT) and, from 1 April 2022, bricks, fly-ash bricks and blocks and earthen or roofing tiles (Notification 4/2022-CT) — though brick makers can use the s.10(2A) route. The Delhi HC in Del Small Ice Cream Manufacturers (2021) declined to strike down the ice-cream exclusion and instead asked the GST Council to reconsider it; we found no later change, so the exclusion stands.

interpretation.h: 3. How the option works and how it ends
p: A registered person opts by filing CMP-02 before the start of the financial year (Rule 3), and the option takes effect from the start of that year (Rule 4); a new registrant can opt in the registration application. On opting in, ITC on stock and capital goods must be reversed (s.18(4), ITC-03). The option is withdrawn voluntarily in CMP-04, and on withdrawal or lapse the person can claim ITC on stock held under s.18(1)(c) within the time in s.18(2).

Lapse is automatic. Under s.10(3) the option ends from the very day aggregate turnover crosses the limit, without any order. The GSTAT Hyderabad Bench applied this in Sri Parameshwara Bricks (reported Aug 2026), where e-way bills showed turnover of about ₹1.96 crore against ₹1.45 crore declared in CMP-08: the dealer was liable at regular rates from the date of crossing. But it also held that, where tax had not been separately charged, the value must be worked out on a tax-inclusive basis under Rule 35 even if the dealer had not asked for it. The Dehradun Bench followed that in a November 2026 order (party not named in reports): a bicycle dealer who wrongly paid 1% after crossing the ₹75 lakh Uttarakhand limit had the differential tax computed on a cum-tax basis, but its ITC claims for FY 2019-20 failed as time-barred under s.16(4) and s.18(2), and the extra general penalties under ss.125 and 75(13) were set aside.

Denial by the officer. Where the officer believes a person was not eligible, Rule 6 requires a notice in CMP-05, a reply in CMP-06 and an order in CMP-07, and Circular 77/51/2018-GST allows the denial to take effect from a past date only through that procedure. Commentary in November 2026 argues that paper notices and orders not uploaded to the portal are defective, because the portal never opens the reply and ITC-01 windows (TaxGuru, R.K. Rastogi) — a useful line in replies, though not yet tested in a reported judgment.

interpretation.h: 4. Section 10(5): tax plus penalty for ineligible use
p: If a person pays composition tax while ineligible, s.10(5) makes him liable for the tax under the normal provisions and a penalty, with ss.73, 74 or (for FY 2024-25 onwards) 74A applying for determination. Two points follow. First, the department must still frame a proper notice and give reasons: the MP HC in Mahendra Singh v. ACST (10 Sep 2025) set aside a non-speaking order against a pan-shop owner and remanded the matter, holding that an advance ruling given to a related person could not be applied to him without independent examination (s.103). Second, the choice between s.73 and s.74 matters — without evidence of fraud or suppression, the penalty should be the lower s.73 penalty, and GSTAT has set aside stacked penalties under ss.125 and 75(13) where s.73 already applied.

A related VAT-era principle is useful by analogy: the Madras HC in Nalini Cycle Mart (reported 18 Sep 2026, TNVAT) held that once the assessing officer accepted turnover below the composition limit, he could not deny the composition rate in the same order. The Karnataka HC took a similar line under KVAT in Oriental Cuisines (2020).

interpretation.h: 5. Compliance once inside the scheme
p: Composition dealers issue a bill of supply, not a tax invoice (s.31(3)(c)), and must mention 'composition taxable person' on bills and display it at the place of business (Rule 5). They pay tax quarterly in CMP-08 by the 18th of the month after the quarter and file GSTR-4 annually (Rule 62). Reverse-charge tax under s.9(3) and (4) is payable in cash in addition to the composition tax, and from 1 November 2026 that includes scrap and used cooking oil bought from unregistered persons. Composition tax itself cannot be recovered from customers and is a cost.

From 1 December 2026, Rule 20 as amended by Notification 08/2026-CT lets a registration be cancelled electronically on the taxpayer's application only if returns — including CMP-08 statements — are filed and dues cleared; otherwise the application goes to an officer. Clients leaving the scheme or closing down should bring CMP-08 and GSTR-4 up to date first.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction with other sections
p: Read s.10 with s.9 (the levy it replaces), s.18 (ITC on entry and exit), s.31(3)(c) (bill of supply), s.39(2) and s.44 (returns), s.52 (e-commerce TCS), s.16(4) (time limit on ITC claimed after exit), and ss.73, 74 and 74A (recovery). Buyers should note that ITC is not available on purchases from composition dealers, and the supplier's GSTR-4 data does not flow into GSTR-2B as creditable tax.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk map
p: The common exposures are: (i) turnover creeping past the limit mid-year — monitor monthly, because liability starts on the day of crossing; (ii) a stray inter-State sale or online sale of services; (iii) e-way bill or bank data showing higher turnover than CMP-08; (iv) related firms under the same PAN, or connected businesses, treated as one for eligibility; (v) manufacturers of notified goods or brick makers using the wrong scheme; and (vi) RCM forgotten because the dealer thinks composition covers everything. In disputes after a lapse, insist on Rule 35 cum-tax valuation and on s.73 rather than s.74 where there is no fraud, and check ITC on stock under s.18(1)(c) before the one-year window closes.

entries.title: Deemed receipt and dividend timing (s.7); assets received by partners on dissolution or reconstitution (s.8)
entries.old1961: Section 7 of the 2025 Act combines 1961-Act s.7 (income deemed to be received) and s.8 (dividend income). Section 8 of the 2025 Act corresponds to 1961-Act s.9B (receipt of capital asset or stock-in-trade by a partner), read with s.45(4) (now s.67(10))
entries.summary: Two timing-and-deeming rules in the basis of charge. Section 7 says when certain income is treated as received or earned: the taxable accretion to a recognised provident fund, the transferred balance, and employer contributions to the NPS are deemed received in the tax year; a final dividend is income of the year it is declared and an interim dividend of the year it is unconditionally made available. Since the Finance Act, 2026, buybacks are no longer dividends, so s.7(2)(a) now covers only s.2(40)(a)–(e). Section 8 carries over the 2021 rule in 1961-Act s.9B: when a partner or member receives a capital asset or stock-in-trade from a firm, LLP or AOP on dissolution or reconstitution, the entity is deemed to have transferred it at fair market value and is taxed on the gain.

text.t: The following incomes shall be deemed to be received in the tax year:— (a) the annual accretion in that year to the balance at the credit of an employee participating in a recognised provident fund, to the extent provided in paragraph 6 of Part A of Schedule XI; (b) the transferred balance in a recognised provident fund, to the extent provided in paragraph 11(4) and (5) of Part A of Schedule XI; (c) the contribution made by the Central Government or any other employer in that year to the account of an employee under a pension scheme mentioned in section 124.

For inclusion in the total income of an assessee,— (a) any dividend declared by a company or distributed or paid by it within the meaning of section 2(40)(a) to (e) shall be deemed to be the income of the tax year in which it is so declared, distributed or paid, as the case may be; (b) any interim dividend shall be deemed to be the income of the tax year in which the amount of such dividend is unconditionally made available by the company to the member who is entitled to it. [Reference to '(e)' substituted by Act 4 of 2026, with effect from 1 April 2026, as shown on the published text]

[In substance] Where a specified person receives during the tax year any capital asset or stock-in-trade, or both, from a specified entity in connection with the dissolution or reconstitution of that entity, the specified entity is deemed to have transferred the asset to the specified person in that year; the resulting profits or gains are chargeable as income of the specified entity under 'Profits and gains of business or profession' or 'Capital gains', in accordance with the Act; and the fair market value of the asset on the date of receipt is deemed to be the full value of the consideration for the deemed transfer.

[Condensed] To remove difficulties in giving effect to this section and section 67(10), the Board may, with the previous approval of the Central Government, issue guidelines, which bind income-tax authorities and the assessee and must be laid before each House of Parliament.

[Condensed] 'Specified entity' means a firm or other association of persons or body of individuals (not being a company or co-operative society); 'specified person' means a partner of the firm or member of the other entity; 'reconstitution' covers one or more partners or members ceasing to be partners or members, new partners or members being admitted while existing ones continue, or a change in the shares of all continuing partners or members.

interpretation.h: 1. What these two sections do — and a numbering trap
p: Both sections are about when and in whose hands income is taxed rather than whether it is income. Section 7 regroups two 1961-Act sections: old s.7 (deemed receipt of provident-fund and pension amounts) is now s.7(1), and old s.8 (dividend timing) is now s.7(2). Section 8 of the 2025 Act is therefore not old s.8: it is the successor to 1961-Act s.9B, inserted by the Finance Act, 2021. When citing old cases, map them carefully — a 1961 's.8 case' on dividends now supports s.7(2), not s.8.
Because the wording of each limb matches the 1961 provision in substance, we carry over the leading 1961-Act (and, for dividends, 1922-Act) case law below and say so for each.

interpretation.h: 2. Section 7(1): amounts deemed received by employees
p: Recognised provident fund. Clause (a) treats the taxable part of the year's accretion to an employee's RPF balance as received in that year, even though the employee cannot draw it. Schedule XI Part A para 6 (the successor to rule 6 of Part A of the Fourth Schedule) decides how much is taxable — broadly the employer's contribution above the prescribed limit and interest credited above the prescribed rate. Clause (b) does the same for the taxable part of a 'transferred balance' when an unrecognised fund becomes recognised.

NPS. Clause (c) treats the employer's contribution to the employee's account under the s.124 pension scheme (old s.80CCD) as received by the employee, so it enters salary; the employee then claims the deduction allowed for employer contributions. Read with the perquisite rule that taxes aggregate employer contributions to PF, NPS and superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh a year (old s.17(2)(vii)), and the separate taxation of PF interest on high employee contributions. Payroll should treat these as income of the year of credit, not of withdrawal.

interpretation.h: 3. Section 7(2): when is a dividend income?
p: The old 'paid' rule. Under s.16(2) of the 1922 Act, dividend was taxed when paid, credited or distributed. In J. Dalmia v. CIT (SC, 1 Apr 1964, 53 ITR 83) the Court held that a board resolution declaring an interim dividend creates no enforceable debt, because the directors can rescind it, and that a dividend is 'paid' when the company discharges its liability and makes the amount unconditionally available to the member. Rampur Distillery & Chemicals v. CIT (SC, 21 Nov 1990) applied the same test and held a dividend in specie taxable in the year it was made available, not when the shares finally reached the shareholder after an injunction.

The statutory rule now. 1961-Act s.8, now s.7(2), changed the rule for final dividends: they are income of the tax year in which they are declared (at the general meeting), whether or not paid in that year. Interim dividends keep the Dalmia test in statutory form — income of the year in which the amount is unconditionally made available. Deemed dividends under s.2(40)(a)–(e) (old s.2(22)(a)–(e): distributions of accumulated profits, bonus debentures or preference shares, distributions on liquidation or capital reduction, and loans or advances to substantial shareholders) are income of the year they are distributed or paid. These 1961 and 1922 precedents are carried over because the language is the same in substance.

Why timing matters today: since dividends became taxable in shareholders' hands, the year decides the rate, the TDS year and the residence status that applies. A dividend declared at an AGM in March but paid in April falls in the earlier tax year for the shareholder.

interpretation.h: 4. Buybacks: out of 'dividend' from 1 April 2026
p: The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 made buyback consideration a deemed dividend from 1 October 2024 (old s.2(22)(f)), and the 2025 Act carried that into s.2(40)(f). The Finance Act, 2026 reversed it: clause (f) is omitted for buybacks on or after 1 April 2026, the gain is taxed as capital gains (s.69(1) per commentary), and promoters face higher effective rates (22% for a domestic-company promoter, 30% for other promoters, per Vinod Kothari Consultants). The cross-reference in s.7(2)(a) was trimmed to '(a) to (e)' to match.

Transition: buybacks between 1 October 2024 and 31 March 2026 remain under the 1961 Act's deemed-dividend rule for FY 2024-25 and 2025-26; only those on or after 1 April 2026 get capital-gains treatment. Check the date the shares were extinguished, not the board approval date — verify the exact transitional wording before advising.

interpretation.h: 5. Section 8: the firm's deemed transfer on reconstitution
p: Background. In Malabar Fisheries v. CIT (SC, 1979) the Court held that distribution of a firm's assets on dissolution is not a transfer, because partners already own the firm's assets jointly. Parliament inserted s.45(4) in 1987 to tax a 'distribution of capital assets on the dissolution of a firm … or otherwise'. Courts then split on 'otherwise': the Bombay HC (A.N. Naik Associates, 2004) applied it to a retiring partner of a continuing firm, while the Karnataka HC Full Bench (Dynamic Enterprises, 2013) held that a payment of money alone was not a distribution of a capital asset. In Mansukh Dyeing & Printing Mills (SC, 2022) the Supreme Court held that revaluing assets and crediting the surplus to partners' capital accounts could be a taxable distribution under old s.45(4).

The 2021 rewrite, now s.8 and s.67(10). The Finance Act, 2021 split the charge: s.9B taxes the firm when a partner receives a capital asset or stock-in-trade, at FMV, as business income or capital gains depending on what the asset was in the firm's hands; and a substituted s.45(4) taxes the firm when a partner receives money or assets exceeding his capital balance, after excluding revaluation and self-generated goodwill credits. The 2025 Act keeps both — s.8 and s.67(10) — and LLPs are covered because they are firms for tax purposes. CBDT Circular 14/2021 (2 Jul 2021) works through examples and applies s.9B first, then s.45(4); Rule 8AB and Form 5C (Rule 50 and Form 27 of the 2026 Rules, per commentary — verify) attribute the s.45(4) gain to the firm's remaining assets for later cost relief.

Prospective only. Chennai ITAT benches have held that the 2021 amendments apply from AY 2021-22 and cannot reach earlier reconstitutions: Gokulakrishna v. DCIT (17 Jun 2025, also holding that compensation from an incoming partner for a reduced profit share was not capital gains, relying on P.N. Panjwani), DCIT v. Sathyabama Ramachandran (23 Sep 2025) and ACIT v. Manikandan (16 Feb 2026). No court has yet applied the 2021 provisions in substance, and none has construed s.8 of the 2025 Act.

interpretation.h: 6. Interaction and transition
p: Read s.7 with s.2(40) (dividend), the salary provisions and Schedule XI (provident funds), s.124 (NPS deduction), and the TDS rules on dividends. Read s.8 with s.67(10)–(11) (money or assets above capital balance), s.67(9) (old s.45(3), contribution of assets by partners), s.72(5) (old s.48(iii)), s.78 (old s.50C) where land is involved, s.92(2)(m) (old s.56(2)(x)) on the partner's side, and s.119 (old s.78) on losses after a change in constitution. Under s.536, reconstitutions and dividends of FY 2025-26 and earlier stay under the 1961 Act; events on or after 1 April 2026 fall under the 2025 Act.

interpretation.h: 7. Practical risk points
p: Common errors: reporting a final dividend in the year of receipt instead of declaration; missing NPS and excess PF contributions in Form 16; treating a post-April 2026 buyback as dividend (or a pre-April 2026 one as capital gains); and, in firms, retiring a partner by handing over property without computing the s.8 gain at FMV or the s.67(10) gain on excess payments. For every admission, retirement or change in profit-sharing ratio, prepare a valuation report, run the s.8 and s.67(10) computations in the order the CBDT circular uses, and file the attribution form by the return due date.

cases.name: CIT v. Mansukh Dyeing & Printing Mills
cases.held: Revaluation surplus credited to partners' capital accounts on reconstitution could be a distribution chargeable under the pre-2021 s.45(4). Governs pre-AY 2021-22 years.

cases.name: CIT v. Dynamic Enterprises
cases.held: Old s.45(4) needed a distribution of a capital asset; payment of money to a retiring partner was not enough. Superseded for AY 2021-22 onwards by the substituted s.45(4), now s.67(10).

cases.name: CIT v. A.N. Naik Associates
cases.held: 'Otherwise' in old s.45(4) is not confined to dissolution; it covers assets given to a retiring partner of a continuing firm.

cases.name: Malabar Fisheries Co. v. CIT
cases.held: Distribution of a firm's assets among partners on dissolution is not a transfer by the firm. Overcome by s.45(4) (1987) and now by s.8 of the 2025 Act.

cases.name: Rampur Distillery & Chemicals Co. Ltd. v. CIT
cases.held: A declared dividend is taxable when paid, credited or distributed — when it is unconditionally available to the members — not when the shareholder later physically receives it. Decided under the 1922 Act; principle carried into s.7(2)(b) for interim dividends.

cases.name: J. Dalmia v. CIT
cases.held: A board resolution declaring an interim dividend is revocable and creates no debt; dividend is 'paid' when unconditionally made available to the member. Codified in 1961-Act s.8(b), now s.7(2)(b); carried over.
